stem: Which animal lives in water?
options: Rabbit
Fish
Cat
Chicken
explanation: Fish live in water. They use fins to swim and gills to take oxygen from water.
theoryLines: Fish are adapted for life in water.
Gills take oxygen from water so fish can breathe.

stem: What happens during photosynthesis?
options: Plants release carbon dioxide and take in oxygen to make energy.
Plants use sunlight and water to make their own food and release oxygen.
Plants absorb only water to produce all the energy they need.
Photosynthesis only takes place in the stem and only during the night.
explanation: During photosynthesis, plants capture energy from sunlight and use it to convert water and carbon dioxide into glucose — a sugar the plant uses for energy and growth. Oxygen is released as a byproduct, which is the oxygen that most living things breathe.
theoryLines: Photosynthesis takes place mainly in the leaves, where cells contain a green pigment called chlorophyll.
Without photosynthesis, there would be no oxygen in the air and no food at the base of the food chain.

stem: What happens when we breathe?
options: Air enters the lungs and never leaves
Air goes in and air goes out
Air only leaves the body and never enters
No gas exchange happens
explanation: When we breathe, air enters through the nose and mouth, and air also leaves the body.
theoryLines: Breathing is essential for life.
Without breathing, we cannot live.

stem: Why record results in a table?
options: To compare measurements and spot patterns
To delete data
To avoid repeating trials
To change the hypothesis after every row
explanation: Organized records make analysis easier.
theoryLines: A table shows data clearly.
Patterns support conclusions.

stem: What describes a fish?
options: It lives in water and breathes with gills
It flies with wings
It has fur and nurses young
It eats only rocks
explanation: A fish is adapted for life in water.
theoryLines: Gills allow breathing in water.
Fins help with swimming.

stem: Why repeat a measurement?
options: To spot mistakes
It is always unnecessary
One measurement is always enough
It changes the goal of the experiment
explanation: Repeating improves reliability.
theoryLines: Random mistakes can happen.
Repeating reduces uncertainty.

stem: What best describes weather?
options: The conditions outside on a given day, such as temperature, rain, or sunshine.
The exact same conditions that repeat every single day throughout the year.
Only the amount of sunshine measured in one particular place.
How hot or cold the Moon is at night.
explanation: Weather describes the conditions in the atmosphere on a particular day, including temperature, rainfall, wind, and cloud cover.
theoryLines: Weather can change from day to day.
Temperature, wind, clouds, and precipitation are all parts of weather.

stem: What is a reasonable link between wind and local sea level at a shore?
options: Strong wind can push water toward or away from the coast
There is usually no link
Wind always flattens waves to zero
Usually only darkness affects the water
explanation: Wind can pile water up along a shore or push it away, changing local water height.
theoryLines: Wind transfers energy to the water surface.
Storms can raise water levels along coasts.

stem: What is an example of a physical change that happens to water?
options: Freezing or evaporating under the right conditions
Water always turning into a new kind of rock
Water never changing at all
Always a chemical reaction
explanation: Freezing, melting, and evaporating change water’s state but keep it as water.
theoryLines: State changes are often physical changes.
Ice, liquid water, and vapor are the same substance.

stem: Which statement correctly describes protecting skin from the Sun?
options: Clothing and shade can reduce risk
Protection is usually unnecessary
Sunlight never affects skin
Usually only water protects skin
explanation: Covering up and staying in shade help protect skin from strong sunlight.
theoryLines: Too much sun can harm skin.
Shade, clothes, and sunscreen are common protections.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the blood vessels that carry blood from the heart to body tissues?
options: Arteries carry blood pumped out of the heart to the body
Veins always carry oxygen-rich blood
Capillaries connect only two nerves
Capillaries create the heartbeat
explanation: Arteries generally carry blood away from the heart; veins return blood to the heart.
theoryLines: The heart pumps blood into arteries.
Capillaries are tiny vessels where exchange with tissues happens.

stem: Which statement correctly describes how breathing works with circulation?
options: Breathing loads blood with oxygen, and blood carries that oxygen to tissues
Blood usually makes oxygen inside lung cells
Muscles take oxygen straight from air
The heart only drains waste and has no link to oxygen
explanation: Gas exchange in the lungs changes the oxygen in blood, which then travels to tissues.
theoryLines: Lungs and blood vessels work as a team.
Cells need oxygen delivered by blood.

stem: Which statement correctly describes Earth’s motion around the Sun?
options: Earth travels around the Sun on a nearly circular elliptical path
Earth stays still while the Moon orbits the Sun with no link to Earth
The Sun orbits Earth once a day with no seasons
Seasons are caused only by daily spin on Earth’s axis
explanation: Earth’s yearly path around the Sun is linked to seasons and changing sunlight angles.
theoryLines: One trip around the Sun takes about one year.
Earth also spins daily to make day and night.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the digestive system at a basic level?
options: It breaks food into smaller parts and absorbs materials into the body
It usually makes oxygen directly from food
It only swaps jobs with the lungs to make red blood
It works only during fast leg movement
explanation: Digestion breaks food down and helps the body absorb nutrients.
theoryLines: Food travels through a digestive pathway.
Absorption moves useful materials into the blood.

stem: What typically describes the life cycle of an insect with complete metamorphosis?
options: Stages such as egg, larva, pupa, and adult that look different
Every stage looks exactly the same
Usually no development stages at all
The adult returns to being an egg with the same shape
explanation: Complete metamorphosis has clear stages with major changes in form.
theoryLines: Butterflies and beetles are examples.
Each stage can use different resources.

stem: What happens in a food web when a basic producer plant is sharply reduced?
options: Energy pathways and consumer dependence can change
Nothing changes because plants do not matter in a web
All animals automatically grow more
Waste disappears with no ecological effect
explanation: Producer plants make organic material that feeds many levels of a food web.
theoryLines: Producers form the base of most food webs.
Losing producers can stress consumers.

stem: What is a correct reason to repeat measurements in the same experiment?
options: Repeats help reveal spread and measurement mistakes
Repeats are always unnecessary if a result looks nice
One trial is always enough no matter the precision needed
Repeats change the original goal for no reason
explanation: Repeating improves reliability and helps show how much results vary.
theoryLines: Random error can appear in single trials.
Consistent repeats strengthen confidence.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the kidneys’ role with blood and body fluids?
options: They filter wastes and help keep fluid balance
They make oxygen for blood
They are usually responsible only for vision
They replace the lungs in gas exchange
explanation: Kidneys filter blood and help regulate fluids and wastes.
theoryLines: Urine carries filtered wastes out of the body.
Kidneys work with the circulatory system.

stem: What usually happens to heart rate when you move from rest to moderate effort for several minutes?
options: It rises gradually to send more oxygen to muscles
It drops immediately with no rise
It stays fixed forever with no link to blood flow
It is set only by room temperature
explanation: During sustained effort the heart works harder to meet oxygen demand.
theoryLines: Active muscles need more oxygenated blood.
Heart rate is a useful fitness indicator.

stem: What is a reasonable link between balanced eating and steady energy during a school day?
options: Timed meals with complex carbohydrates and protein support steadier energy
Skipping breakfast always improves focus with no exceptions
Only quick sugar is a source of steady energy
Lots of coffee usually replaces sleep with no effects
explanation: Regular, balanced meals help keep energy more stable through the day.
theoryLines: The body needs fuel from food.
Sleep and hydration also support energy and focus.

stem: What correctly describes how the sky looks during a clear day?
options: The Sun appears to move across the sky, and shadows change
The Moon always stays fixed with no motion
Stars disappear at noon because of desk height
Time of day has no link to shadow direction
explanation: As the day goes on, the Sun’s position in the sky changes and shadows shift.
theoryLines: Earth’s rotation makes the Sun appear to move.
Shadow length and direction change with time.

stem: What describes the Moon in the night sky in a simple observation?
options: It looks like a bright disk that can be seen without special tools
It is always full every evening with no cycle
It shines with its own light like the Sun
It is usually visible only at noon
explanation: The Moon reflects sunlight and appears in changing shapes through its cycle.
theoryLines: Moon phases change over about a month.
The Moon does not make its own light.

stem: What is a safe way to observe the Sun during the day?
options: Use a proper solar filter or a supervised projection or shade method
Stare directly for a long time with no protection
Use a regular telescope with no filter
Usually point a laser at the Sun
explanation: Looking at the Sun can hurt eyes. Use approved filters and adult supervision.
theoryLines: Sunlight is intense enough to damage vision.
Safe solar viewing needs special tools.

stem: Why is it important to wash hands before eating?
options: To reduce germs that could enter the body
So hands are always dry
Usually only to strengthen muscles
Usually so we do not need sleep
explanation: Handwashing reduces germs that can travel into the digestive system.
theoryLines: Germs can live on hands.
Clean hands help keep you healthier.

stem: Why is it helpful to get enough sleep at night?
options: To let the body rest and recover
So we do not need to eat
So hair grows faster
Usually so we do not breathe
explanation: Sleep supports growth and recovery.
theoryLines: Rest helps the body and brain.
Kids need enough sleep to feel ready for the day.

stem: Why should you wear a helmet when you ride a bike?
options: A helmet helps protect your brain if you fall.
A helmet makes your bike go faster by itself.
A helmet replaces the need for brakes.
A helmet feeds your muscles.
explanation: Your brain is inside your skull. A helmet adds extra protection if you bump your head.
theoryLines: The brain controls thinking and movement.
Safety gear helps prevent injuries.

stem: Which animal lives in water and breathes with gills?
options: A fish
A cat
A chicken
A butterfly
explanation: Fish live in water. Gills help them take oxygen from the water.
theoryLines: Different animals live in different habitats.
Gills work underwater.

stem: Why do fish have gills?
options: Gills help fish take oxygen from water.
Gills help fish bark like dogs.
Gills help fish make honey.
Gills help fish grow feathers.
explanation: Fish need oxygen just like we do. Gills pull oxygen out of the water so fish can breathe underwater.
theoryLines: Land animals usually breathe with lungs.
Water animals may use gills.

stem: Why are many bats active at night?
options: Night can make finding food safer or easier for them.
They melt in sunlight like ice cream.
They can only fly when it snows.
They are afraid of trees.
explanation: Bats are often nocturnal. Night activity can help them hunt insects and avoid some dangers.
theoryLines: Nocturnal animals are active at night.
Different animals are active at different times.

stem: What is one main role of the skeleton?
options: It supports the body and protects organs like the brain and heart.
It digests sugar in the mouth only.
It senses smells better than the nose.
It makes all of your memories.
explanation: Bones give shape and support. The skull protects the brain, and the rib cage helps protect the heart and lungs.
theoryLines: The skeleton is a living framework.
Joints let bones move where they meet.

stem: Why is eating a variety of healthy foods important?
options: Different foods give different nutrients your body needs.
One candy bar gives every nutrient forever.
Food is only for changing hair color.
People do not need nutrients at all.
explanation: Nutrients include proteins, vitamins, minerals, and more. A balanced diet helps growth, energy, and health.
theoryLines: No single food has everything you need.
Fruits, vegetables, grains, and proteins each help in different ways.

stem: Why is warming up before hard exercise helpful?
options: It gently prepares muscles and joints for activity.
It freezes your muscles solid.
It removes the need to breathe.
It turns sweat into glue.
explanation: A warm-up increases blood flow and loosens muscles. That can help you move better and lower injury risk.
theoryLines: Start activity slowly, then go harder.
Stretching and light movement are common warm-ups.

stem: Why do scientists often repeat an experiment?
options: Repeating helps check whether results are reliable.
Repeating erases the need for any data.
Repeating makes safety rules unnecessary.
Repeating turns opinions into magic spells.
explanation: One trial might be a lucky accident. Similar results across repeats make findings more trustworthy.
theoryLines: Reliable results can be repeated.
More trials can reveal mistakes or chance differences.

stem: Why do scientists keep experiment conditions the same when possible?
options: So differences in results are more likely caused by the variable being tested
So no one needs to measure anything
So safety rules can be ignored
So hypotheses become facts automatically
explanation: Controlled conditions make comparisons fair. Then you can better link the changed variable to the outcome.
theoryLines: Same conditions support fair tests.
Write down the conditions you used.

stem: What major change happens in a butterfly's life cycle?
options: It goes through stages, including caterpillar and chrysalis, before becoming an adult butterfly.
It stays a caterpillar forever with no changes.
It hatches as a mammal with fur.
It skips being young and starts as a tree.
explanation: Butterflies metamorphose. The caterpillar feeds and grows, then transforms inside a chrysalis into a winged adult.
theoryLines: Life cycles show how animals grow and change.
Different stages may use different foods or habitats.

stem: What do plants make during photosynthesis?
options: Food (sugar) using light, water, and carbon dioxide
Rocks using only darkness
Plastic using saltwater only
Electricity using sand
explanation: In photosynthesis, plants capture light energy and build sugar. Oxygen is released as a useful byproduct.
theoryLines: Leaves are major sites of photosynthesis.
Animals depend on plant-made food energy.

stem: What happens to most plants without enough water?
options: They wilt and may die if the drought continues.
They instantly become desert cameras.
They stop needing sunlight forever.
They turn into mushrooms overnight.
explanation: Water keeps plant cells firm and supports photosynthesis. Without it, leaves droop and life processes slow or stop.
theoryLines: Wilting is an early water-stress sign.
Different plants tolerate drought differently.

stem: What happens to blood when it travels through the lungs?
options: It picks up oxygen and drops off carbon dioxide.
It turns into stomach acid.
It stores leftover bones.
It becomes plant sap.
explanation: In the lungs, gas exchange occurs. Blood gains oxygen for the body and releases carbon dioxide to be exhaled.
theoryLines: The heart sends blood to the lungs and body.
Oxygen-rich blood fuels active cells.

stem: What do the kidneys help do?
options: Filter waste from the blood and help make urine
Pump air into the ears
Digest food using chlorophyll
Grow new skull bones each hour
explanation: Kidneys clean the blood by removing wastes and extra water. The wastes leave the body as urine.
theoryLines: Healthy kidneys support internal balance.
Drinking enough water helps body systems, including the kidneys.

stem: What belongs in a data table during an experiment?
options: Organized measurements and observations from each trial
Only jokes with no numbers
Only the title of your favorite movie
Only guesses with no recording of results
explanation: Tables capture what happened in a structured way. Labels, units, and trial numbers keep data usable.
theoryLines: Good records support analysis.
Others should be able to read your table.

stem: Why do scientists often repeat the same trial many times?
options: To build confidence that results are not just a one-time accident
To ignore safety rules
To change two variables secretly
To avoid writing units
explanation: Repeats reveal consistency. Outliers become clearer, and average trends are more trustworthy.
theoryLines: Reliability grows with careful repetition.
Report all honest trials, not only favorites.

stem: What is watching birds at a feeder without changing anything mainly called?
options: Observation
An experiment that changes a variable
A control group chemical test
A measurement of mass with a balance
explanation: Observation gathers information carefully. An experiment would add a planned change, such as feeder type, to test an effect.
theoryLines: Both skills are valuable in science.
Questions determine whether you only observe or also experiment.

stem: What is an insect that looks like a leaf most likely using?
options: Camouflage to avoid being eaten
Echolocation to find nectar
Gills to breathe on land
Migration to leave Earth's orbit
explanation: Looking like a leaf hides the insect from predators. Camouflage is a defensive adaptation.
theoryLines: Appearance can improve survival odds.
Predators may also use camouflage when hunting.

stem: The kidneys are part of which body job?
options: Filtering wastes from blood
Pumping air into feathers
Making chlorophyll for skin
Storing pollen in bone marrow
explanation: Kidneys clean blood and help control water and salt balance. Wastes leave as urine.
theoryLines: Excretion removes harmful leftovers.
Organ systems cooperate to keep conditions stable.

stem: What happens to your lungs when you inhale?
options: Fill with air so oxygen can enter the blood
Fill with food for digestion
Pump blood to the feet only
Produce urine for the kidneys
explanation: Inhaling brings fresh air into tiny air sacs. Oxygen crosses into blood while carbon dioxide exits.
theoryLines: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs.
Respiratory health affects energy and endurance.

stem: Why does staying hydrated help during long sports practices?
options: Water lost in sweat must be replaced for the body to work well.
Water freezes muscles so they cannot move.
Water removes oxygen from blood on purpose.
Water stops nerves from sending any signals.
explanation: Sweating cools you but reduces body water. Replacing fluids helps circulation, temperature control, and performance.
theoryLines: Thirst and dark urine can signal low fluid levels.
Plan water breaks in hot weather.

stem: Why do scientists or doctors measure a person's pulse?
options: To learn about heart rate and how hard the circulatory system is working
To measure exact hair length in millimeters only
To learn stomach enzyme brand names
To count the number of bones grown that hour
explanation: Pulse is a window into heart activity. It can show rest, exercise response, or possible health concerns.
theoryLines: Heart rate is beats per minute.
Context matters when interpreting pulse.

stem: Why is warming up properly before sprinting useful?
options: Increases blood flow and prepares muscles for sudden hard effort
Removes lactic acid by stopping breathing
Converts muscle into bone for speed
Eliminates the need for shoes and safety
explanation: Warm tissues move more freely and receive more blood. That preparation can improve performance and reduce injury risk.
theoryLines: Warm-ups are part of smart training.
Intensity should rise gradually.

stem: What should a lab log include?
options: Procedures, observations, measurements, and dates
Only emojis with no data
Only the final guess, with methods erased
Only a list of friends' names
explanation: Detailed logs let you and others understand what was done and found. They support honest analysis and replication.
theoryLines: Science depends on clear communication.
Write observations as they happen.

stem: Why are gills useful for many aquatic animals?
options: Allow many aquatic animals to take oxygen from water
Let land mammals photosynthesize
Store pollen for winter nests
Turn carbon dioxide into fur
explanation: Water holds dissolved oxygen. Gills extract it so fish and some other aquatic animals can breathe underwater.
theoryLines: Gas exchange structures fit the environment.
Lungs are common for breathing air.

stem: What is an important job of the kidneys?
options: Filter waste from the blood and help make urine
Pump oxygen straight into the ears
Store sunlight under the skin
Heat the body by burning bones
explanation: Kidneys clean the blood by removing wastes and extra water, which leave the body as urine.
theoryLines: Kidneys are part of the excretory system.
Healthy kidneys help keep blood chemistry balanced.

stem: Why is warming up before hard exercise helpful?
options: It gently prepares muscles for stronger activity
It removes the need for oxygen
It turns muscles into bone
It stops the heart from pumping
explanation: A warm-up increases blood flow and loosens muscles so they are ready for harder movement and less likely to strain.
theoryLines: Warm muscles work more safely during exercise.
Light activity before a workout prepares the body.

stem: Why do scientists change only one variable at a time in a fair test?
options: So they can tell what caused the result
So every measurement becomes identical forever
So they never need to record data
So the experiment finishes without tools
explanation: If too many things change at once, you cannot know which change caused the outcome.
theoryLines: A fair test keeps most conditions the same.
The independent variable is the one you purposely change.

stem: Why should you write down what happens during an experiment?
options: A clear log helps you remember and share results
Notes make the equipment heavier
Writing replaces the need for safety
Logs turn water into ice instantly
explanation: Recording observations and measurements lets you check your work and compare results later.
theoryLines: Scientists keep careful records of procedures and data.
Good notes make experiments easier to repeat.

stem: Why do scientists often repeat an experiment?
options: To check whether the results are reliable
To invent a new planet each time
To avoid measuring anything
To erase all earlier evidence
explanation: Repeating a test helps show whether results happen again and are not just a lucky accident.
theoryLines: Reliable results can be repeated under similar conditions.
Repeating trials reduces the chance of a one-time mistake.

stem: What is the most important reason to follow safety rules in a lab?
options: To protect people and prevent accidents
To make experiments finish faster only
To avoid writing any observations
To keep results secret from everyone
explanation: Safety rules reduce harm from spills, heat, sharp tools, and other lab risks.
theoryLines: Wear safety gear when a procedure calls for it.
Ask an adult before using unfamiliar lab materials.

stem: What usually happens when predators become scarce in an ecosystem?
options: Prey populations may grow larger for a while
All plants instantly disappear
Rain stops falling forever
Every animal turns into a producer
explanation: Predators help control prey numbers. With fewer predators, prey can increase until food or space runs short.
theoryLines: Predator and prey populations affect each other.
Balance in ecosystems depends on many living links.

stem: Why is it helpful when many different animals live in a place?
options: A variety of living things helps keep nature systems healthier
Rain becomes unnecessary
Food disappears forever
Light stops reaching Earth
explanation: Biodiversity means many kinds of living things. Together they support food webs and healthier habitats.
theoryLines: Different animals play different roles in nature.
Protecting habitats protects many species.

stem: Why do graphs need clear labels on the axes?
options: So readers know what the numbers and categories mean
So the graph can hide all of the data
So hypotheses become unnecessary
So experiments never need measuring
explanation: Axis labels tell people what was measured and how to read the graph correctly.
theoryLines: A graph is a picture of data.
Clear labels make science communication easier.

stem: What should you do if one measurement looks very different from the others?
options: Check it again and think about possible mistakes
Always delete all of your data
Change the hypothesis to match one odd number only
Stop using units forever
explanation: An outlier may be an error. Rechecking helps you decide whether to keep, fix, or explain the unusual result.
theoryLines: Careful checking improves data quality.
Repeating a measurement can reveal mistakes.

stem: Why do scientists use a control group?
options: To compare what happens without the tested change
To avoid collecting any evidence
To make every trial identical by magic
To replace measuring with guessing
explanation: A control group shows the normal result, so you can see the effect of the change you tested.
theoryLines: Comparison makes experimental results meaningful.
Controls help scientists trust their conclusions.

stem: What happens to a plant when it does not get enough water?
options: The plant wilts, stops growing, and may eventually die.
The plant grows taller to find rain coming from nearby mountains.
The plant produces more leaves to collect moisture from the air.
The plant grows its roots sideways toward other nearby plants.
explanation: Water is essential for plants. Without enough water, a plant cannot carry out photosynthesis, its cells lose pressure, and it wilts. It may die if water is not provided.

stem: What is the main role of teeth in digestion?
options: To chew and break food into smaller pieces, making it easier to swallow and digest.
To breathe oxygen in and out of the mouth.
To pump blood through the digestive system.
To cool down hot food before you swallow it.
explanation: Teeth break food into smaller pieces through chewing. This mechanical breakdown is the first step in digestion and makes it easier for the stomach and intestines to process food.

stem: What is one clear difference between most birds and fish?
options: Birds have feathers, while fish have scales and gills
Birds breathe only with gills underwater
Fish grow feathers for flight
Neither group needs oxygen
explanation: Birds are feathered animals that usually breathe air with lungs. Fish typically have scales and use gills in water.
theoryLines: Animal groups share sets of traits.
Comparing traits helps classify living things.

stem: What do the kidneys do in the body?
options: They filter wastes from the blood
They pump air into the ears
They store sunlight under the skin
They digest food in the mouth
explanation: Kidneys clean the blood by removing wastes that leave the body as urine.
theoryLines: Kidneys help keep blood balanced.
The excretory system removes wastes.

stem: Why is eating a balanced diet important?
options: Different foods give the body a mix of nutrients it needs
Only one food group is ever useful
Food is unrelated to energy
Balanced meals stop all growth
explanation: A balanced diet includes a variety of foods that supply energy, vitamins, minerals, and other nutrients.
theoryLines: Fruits, vegetables, grains, proteins, and dairy can all play roles.
Good nutrition supports growth and health.

stem: What is the brain's main role in the body?
options: It is the control center for thinking, sensing, and movement
It digests all food by itself
It pumps blood like a second heart
It makes sunlight for the eyes
explanation: The brain receives information, makes decisions, and sends signals that guide the body.
theoryLines: The brain is part of the nervous system.
Learning and memory happen in the brain.

stem: What does it mean when another team can repeat your experiment and get a similar result?
options: Your result is more likely to be reliable
Your hypothesis must be false forever
Measuring tools are no longer needed
The experiment had no variables
explanation: Replication means others can get similar results, which builds confidence in the findings.
theoryLines: Science becomes stronger when results can be repeated.
Clear methods help other people replicate a test.

stem: What is one main job of a fish's fins?
options: Helping the fish move and stay balanced in water
Making feathers for flight
Producing pollen for flowers
Filtering blood like kidneys
explanation: Fins help fish swim, turn, and keep steady in the water.
theoryLines: Fish are adapted for swimming.
Body shape and fins work together in water.

stem: Which statement correctly compares birds and fish?
options: Most birds breathe air with lungs; fish usually use gills
Fish have feathers and fly long distances
Birds take oxygen only from underwater gills
Neither group can move from place to place
explanation: Birds and fish are both animals, but they have different body features for different habitats.
theoryLines: Lungs and gills are different ways to get oxygen.
Traits help scientists sort animals into groups.

stem: What happens to light after it enters your eyes?
options: Signals travel to the brain so you can see
The light digests food in the stomach
The light turns into sound in the ears
The light becomes blood in the heart
explanation: Eyes detect light and send nerve signals to the brain, which builds the images you see.
theoryLines: Vision depends on both the eyes and the brain.
The optic nerve carries visual signals.

stem: Why do you breathe faster after hard exercise?
options: The body needs more oxygen for working muscles
The stomach suddenly stops digesting
Bones need less blood
The eyes stop sending signals
explanation: Active muscles use more oxygen, so breathing and heart rate increase to deliver it.
theoryLines: Exercise raises the body's oxygen demand.
Faster breathing helps bring in more air.

stem: Why should you wash your hands before eating?
options: To help remove germs that could make you sick
To make food taste colder
To stop bones from growing
To replace brushing your teeth
explanation: Clean hands reduce the chance of spreading harmful microbes to your mouth and food.
theoryLines: Handwashing is a simple health habit.
Soap and water help remove dirt and germs.

stem: What does a balanced diet provide?
options: A mix of nutrients the body needs to stay healthy
Only sugar and nothing else
A way to avoid all water
Energy that never comes from food
explanation: Eating different healthy foods supplies proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, and minerals.
theoryLines: Variety helps cover nutrient needs.
Good food choices support growth and energy.

stem: What often happens to your pulse after running hard?
options: It becomes faster
It disappears completely
It turns into a smell signal
It measures only eye color
explanation: During activity the heart beats faster, so the pulse rate rises.
theoryLines: Pulse is a sign of heart rate.
Resting brings the pulse back down.

stem: Why should you wear a helmet for biking or skating?
options: To help protect your head from injury
To make hearing louder
To digest food faster
To stop blood from circulating
explanation: A helmet cushions the head if you fall and helps prevent serious injuries.
theoryLines: The brain is protected by the skull and by safe habits.
Safety gear reduces risk during sports.

stem: What do the kidneys help remove from the blood?
options: Wastes that leave the body as urine
All of the body's oxygen forever
Every red blood cell permanently
Only unused sunlight
explanation: Kidneys filter blood and help form urine that carries wastes away.
theoryLines: Excretion removes wastes from the body.
Healthy kidneys support clean, balanced blood.

stem: Why is breakfast helpful for many kids?
options: It gives energy to start the day
It stops all learning at school
It removes the need to drink water
It freezes muscles until night
explanation: Eating in the morning provides fuel after a night without food.
theoryLines: Food supplies energy for activity and thinking.
A healthy breakfast can include fruits, grains, and protein foods.

stem: Which foods are especially helpful for strong bones because they provide calcium?
options: Milk, yogurt, and other calcium-rich foods
Only candy and soda
Only dry paper
Only pure salt water
explanation: Calcium helps build and maintain strong bones and teeth.
theoryLines: Dairy foods are common calcium sources.
Some leafy greens and fortified foods also provide calcium.

stem: Why are fruits and vegetables helpful in a daily diet?
options: They provide vitamins, minerals, and fiber
They remove all need for water
They replace oxygen in the lungs
They turn bones into rubber
explanation: Fruits and vegetables supply nutrients that support health and growth.
theoryLines: Colorful produce often means a variety of nutrients.
Fiber helps digestion.

stem: Why is good posture helpful for your back?
options: It supports the spine and can reduce strain
It stops bones from existing
It removes the need for muscles
It freezes joints permanently
explanation: Sitting and standing tall helps the backbone carry your body weight more comfortably.
theoryLines: The spine supports the head and trunk.
Strong core muscles also help posture.

stem: What best describes the texture of a sponge when you touch it?
options: It is soft and can be squeezed easily
It is hard and cannot be bent or compressed
It is rough and sharp like coarse sandpaper
It feels like cold, smooth metal
explanation: A sponge is a soft material that can be easily squeezed and compressed because it contains many tiny holes filled with air.

stem: What happens to a soft sponge when you press down hard on it?
options: It changes shape while pressed but returns to its original shape when released
It breaks apart into tiny pieces that cannot be put back together
It hardens and becomes as stiff as a piece of metal
It always stays exactly the same shape no matter how hard you press
explanation: A sponge is a soft, elastic material. When you press it, it compresses and changes shape, but it springs back to its original form when you let go.

stem: What does the sun give us during the daytime?
options: Light and warmth that let us see and keep Earth at a comfortable temperature
Cold winds and heavy rain that fall from the sky
Fresh drinking water that drips down from the clouds
Gravity that pulls all objects down to the ground
explanation: The sun provides light and heat during the day. Its light lets us see, and its warmth keeps the Earth at temperatures that support life.

stem: What can you often see in the night sky?
options: The Moon and stars
Only ocean waves
Only underground roots
Only classroom chalkboards
explanation: At night the sky looks dark, and the Moon and stars are easier to notice.
theoryLines: The Moon reflects sunlight.
Stars are distant suns that look like points of light.

stem: What can thick clouds do to sunlight during the day?
options: Block some light and make the ground look dimmer
Turn the sun into the Moon
Stop Earth from rotating
Make shadows impossible forever
explanation: Cloud cover can reduce the sunlight that reaches the ground, so a day may look gray and less bright.
theoryLines: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals.
Weather can change how much sunlight we receive.

stem: Why do we wear a raincoat when it rains?
options: To keep our body dry and protected from getting wet in the rain.
To see the Moon more clearly through the rainy clouds.
To help Earth absorb rainwater faster into the ground.
To make rain fall more slowly and gently.
explanation: We wear a raincoat so rain does not soak our body and clothes. The waterproof material keeps us dry and protected while it is raining.
theoryLines: Waterproof materials make water run off instead of soaking in.
We choose clothes that match the weather to stay comfortable and protected.

stem: Why are trees in a park helpful?
options: They give shade, homes for animals, and fresher air
They remove all need for water on Earth
They stop seasons from changing
They turn playgrounds into deserts
explanation: Trees provide shade, shelter, and oxygen while making parks nicer places to visit.
theoryLines: Plants support healthy environments.
Parks need care so living things can thrive.

stem: What happens to a puddle of water on a warm, sunny day?
options: The heat from the sun causes the water to evaporate and turn into water vapor in the air
The water sinks straight down into the ground and is gone forever
The puddle grows larger because sunlight creates extra water
Sunlight hardens the surface of the puddle so it stays as a permanent solid
explanation: Heat from the sun gives water molecules enough energy to escape from the liquid surface and rise into the air as invisible water vapor. This is called evaporation.

stem: Why is recycling paper helpful?
options: It saves materials and can reduce waste
It makes trees disappear faster on purpose
It pollutes rivers automatically
It stops people from reading books
explanation: Recycling paper reuses fiber so fewer new resources may be needed and less trash piles up.
theoryLines: Paper comes from plant materials.
Recycling is one way to care for the environment.

stem: What happens during a phase change of water?
options: Water changes form, such as liquid to gas, without becoming a new substance
Water turns into a brand-new metal element
Water permanently loses all hydrogen
Water becomes living tissue
explanation: Melting, freezing, evaporation, and condensation change water's state, not its chemical identity.
theoryLines: H2O stays water in solid, liquid, or gas form.
Heat energy drives many phase changes.

stem: What is recycling?
options: Burying everything in backyard soil with no sorting
Using old materials again to make new products
Piling waste forever in one place with no recycling
Crushing mixed materials together with no prep for reuse
explanation: Recycling turns used materials such as plastic, paper, and glass into new products instead of throwing them away.
theoryLines: Recycling helps protect the environment.
It reduces waste and saves resources.

stem: What is a control group in an experiment?
options: A group that usually never changes for any reason
A group in the experiment that you leave unchanged so you can compare results
A group that always changes
An experiment with only one group and no comparison
explanation: A control group is left unchanged so you can compare and see what really caused the result.
theoryLines: A control group is part of a strong experiment.
It helps you understand what caused the outcome.

stem: Why is it important to do experiments?
options: Because an opinion is enough without testing a real case
To learn about the world, test ideas, and understand how things work
Only to pass time with no clear experiment question
To watch once and rely on memory with no notes or repeats
explanation: Experiments help us learn about the world, test ideas, understand how things work, and discover new things.
theoryLines: Experiments are a scientific way to learn.
They help students think like scientists.

stem: What is inside clouds?
options: Completely dry air with no water
Tiny water droplets
Dust with no liquid water
Strong wind with no moisture
explanation: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals. When they get heavy, rain can fall.
theoryLines: Clouds form when water vapor condenses.
When droplets grow heavy, rain or snow can fall.

stem: What is recycling?
options: Putting paper and used oil in the same trash bag with no sorting
Using old materials again to make new things
Leaving unsorted waste in the yard for a long time
Burning mixed yard waste with uncontrolled smoke
explanation: Recycling means using old materials again to make new products instead of throwing them away.
theoryLines: Recycling helps protect the environment.
It reduces waste and saves resources.

stem: What are clouds?
options: Dry air with no visible droplets
Tiny water droplets or ice crystals in the atmosphere
Dust alone with no moisture
Fast wind with no gathered droplets
explanation: Clouds are tiny water droplets or ice crystals in the air. When they get heavy, rain or snow can fall.
theoryLines: Clouds form when water vapor condenses.
There are many kinds of clouds.

stem: What is a control group?
options: A group where you change every factor at once with no baseline for comparison
A group you compare other results against
A group measured only at the end with no starting treatment
A group meant to copy the main result with no baseline
explanation: A control group is left unchanged so you can compare results and see what made the difference.
theoryLines: It helps you understand what caused the outcome.
It is an important part of a science experiment.

stem: What causes daytime on Earth?
options: Earth rotating so that our side faces toward the Sun.
The Sun moving to the far side of the Moon each night.
The Moon blocking sunlight and bouncing it back toward Earth.
Earth staying still while the Sun circles around it.
explanation: Earth spins on its axis, making one full turn every 24 hours. When the side of Earth where you live faces the Sun, it is daytime. When that side faces away from the Sun, it is nighttime.
theoryLines: Earth's rotation is what creates the 24-hour cycle of day and night.
The Sun itself does not move around Earth — Earth's spin makes it look like the Sun rises and sets.

stem: What is a basic example of recycling?
options: Collecting bottles for recycling
Burning trash with no sorting
Throwing everything in the same bin
Never sorting materials
explanation: Recycling means collecting used materials so they can be made into new products.
theoryLines: Sorting materials helps recycling work.
Recycling can save resources and reduce landfill waste.

stem: What is an important step before repeating a measurement in the same experiment?
options: Clearly define what stays the same and what changes
Change every variable together
Erase earlier results without recording them
Make sure there is no planned variable
explanation: In a controlled experiment, change one variable and keep other conditions as steady as possible.
theoryLines: Clear variables make repeats meaningful.
Good planning comes before measuring.

stem: Which explanation best links pulse to body activity?
options: During hard physical effort, heart rate often rises to supply muscles
Pulse is always the same no matter the activity
The heart stops during effort
Pulse depends only on room temperature, not muscles
explanation: During exercise the body needs more oxygen, so the heart usually beats faster.
theoryLines: Working muscles need more blood flow.
Pulse rate is a useful activity clue.

stem: What can a simple weather log include?
options: Approximate temperature, cloud clues, and wind direction
Only the observer’s shirt color
Only the number of classroom windows
Only the teacher’s name, with no link to the sky
explanation: Weather records use observations that others can repeat and compare.
theoryLines: Temperature, clouds, and wind are common weather measures.
Logs help spot patterns over days.

stem: How can you help keep your teeth healthy?
options: Brush your teeth and avoid lots of sugary snacks.
Never brush your teeth at all.
Only wash your hair each morning.
Sleep with candy under your pillow.
explanation: Brushing removes food and germs that can hurt teeth. Limiting sugary snacks also helps prevent cavities.
theoryLines: Teeth help you chew food.
Healthy teeth need daily care.

stem: Why does your pulse feel faster after you run?
options: Your heart is beating faster to send blood to your muscles.
Your bones are melting from heat.
Your skin stops sensing touch.
Your stomach turns into a lung.
explanation: Running uses a lot of energy. Your heart speeds up so blood can carry more oxygen to working muscles.
theoryLines: Pulse is the beat of blood from the heart.
You can feel a pulse on your wrist or neck.

stem: What is an important job of leaves?
options: They help the plant make food using sunlight.
They dig tunnels under roads.
They pump blood through the plant.
They chew insects for dinner.
explanation: Leaves catch sunlight. Plants use light, water, and air to make sugar food in a process called photosynthesis.
theoryLines: Green leaves often do photosynthesis.
Food made in leaves feeds the whole plant.

stem: What is one important role of fruit on a plant?
options: Fruit helps protect and spread seeds.
Fruit turns the plant into a rock.
Fruit stops the plant from needing light.
Fruit digests food for animals' bones.
explanation: Fruits hold seeds. Animals may eat fruit and carry seeds to new places, helping plants spread.
theoryLines: Seeds grow into new plants.
Fruit is part of a plant's life cycle.

stem: In a simple food chain, what do plants provide?
options: Food energy for animals that eat them
Only plastic for packaging
Electricity for televisions
Clouds made of sugar
explanation: A food chain shows who eats whom. Plants make food energy that plant-eaters use first.
theoryLines: Energy moves from plants to animals.
Food chains start with producers.

stem: What is digestion?
options: Breaking food into smaller parts the body can use
Pumping blood through the lungs only
Growing new teeth from sunlight
Turning bones into water
explanation: Digestion starts in the mouth and continues in the stomach and intestines. Nutrients then move into the blood.
theoryLines: Teeth help begin digestion by chewing.
The digestive system turns food into usable fuel.

stem: What is one important job of blood?
options: It carries oxygen, nutrients, and waste around the body.
It digests rocks in the stomach.
It grows feathers on your arms.
It replaces the need for a brain.
explanation: Blood is a transport system. It delivers what cells need and carries away wastes.
theoryLines: The heart keeps blood moving.
Blood travels in blood vessels.

stem: Why can breakfast help many kids at school?
options: It gives energy and nutrients after a night without eating.
It makes homework finish itself.
It replaces the need to drink water all day.
It turns books into toys.
explanation: After sleep, your body needs fuel again. A good breakfast can support focus, energy, and learning.
theoryLines: Food provides energy for brain and body.
Regular meals support healthy habits.

stem: What does your pulse tell you?
options: How fast your heart is beating
How tall you will be next year
What color your eyes will become
How many teeth you will grow tomorrow
explanation: Each heartbeat pushes blood, making a pulse you can feel. Counting pulse beats shows heart rate.
theoryLines: Pulse is linked to heart activity.
Heart rate changes with rest and exercise.

stem: Why do experiments often include a control?
options: A control is a comparison that helps show what the change caused.
A control is a prize for finishing early.
A control deletes all measurements.
A control means changing every factor at once.
explanation: A control setup stays unchanged on purpose. Comparing it with the test setup shows the effect of the variable you changed.
theoryLines: Controls make tests fairer.
Compare results to see real differences.

stem: Why is changing two variables at the same time a problem in a fair test?
options: You cannot tell which change caused the result.
It makes the experiment perfectly fair.
It removes the need for any control.
It guarantees the same result every time.
explanation: If light and water both change, either one—or both—might explain the outcome. Change one main variable at a time.
theoryLines: Fair tests isolate one factor.
Keep other conditions the same.

stem: Why should measurements include units?
options: Units tell what the number means, like centimeters or grams.
Units are only for decoration.
Units make numbers unnecessary.
Units erase differences between trials.
explanation: A number without units is unclear. Saying "5 centimeters" is different from "5 grams."
theoryLines: Always label measurements with units.
Matching units helps you compare data.

stem: Why are bees important to many flowering plants?
options: Bees help pollinate flowers as they collect nectar.
Bees turn flowers into plastic.
Bees stop seeds from ever forming.
Bees replace sunlight for plants.
explanation: Pollen sticks to bees and moves between flowers. Pollination helps plants make fruits and seeds.
theoryLines: Pollinators support food webs and farms.
Protecting bees helps ecosystems.

stem: What do fins help a fish do?
options: Swim, steer, and keep balance in water
Walk on land like a horse
Make pollen for flowers
Pump blood without a heart
explanation: Different fins have jobs like moving forward, turning, and staying upright. Together they help fish move well underwater.
theoryLines: Body structures match the environment.
Water animals need ways to move through water.

stem: Why should a science log include the date?
options: Dates help you track when observations were made and compare changes over time.
Dates make plants grow faster by themselves.
Dates replace the need for measurements.
Dates erase experimental errors.
explanation: Time stamps keep records organized. You can see growth, weather links, or which trial came first.
theoryLines: Clear notebooks support good science.
Details make data useful later.

stem: Why are leaves especially important for a plant?
options: Capture light and help make food for the plant
Chase insects across the ground
Pump blood to animal hearts
Store electricity for cities
explanation: Most photosynthesis happens in leaves. That food energy supports roots, stems, flowers, and fruits.
theoryLines: Leaf shape and arrangement can affect light capture.
Green plants rely on leaf function.

stem: Where does digestion of food begin?
options: In the mouth, where chewing and saliva start breaking food down
Only in the hair follicles
Only in the fingernails
Only in the outer ear
explanation: Teeth grind food and saliva begins chemical breakdown. Digestion continues in the stomach and intestines.
theoryLines: Mechanical and chemical digestion work together.
The digestive tract is a long pathway for food.

stem: Why are teeth important for digestion?
options: They break food into smaller pieces that are easier to swallow and digest.
They filter wastes from the blood like kidneys.
They carry nerve signals to the toes only.
They produce red blood cells.
explanation: Chewing increases food's surface area so enzymes can work better. Different teeth shapes suit cutting and grinding.
theoryLines: Dental care supports good nutrition.
Digestion is harder with very large unchewed bites.

stem: If your pulse is faster, what is usually true?
options: Your heart is beating more times per minute.
Your bones have disappeared.
Your skin has stopped sensing touch.
Your stomach has become a lung.
explanation: Pulse rate matches heart rate. Exercise, excitement, or fever can raise how often the heart beats.
theoryLines: You can measure pulse at wrist or neck.
Resting rates are usually lower than exercise rates.

stem: What is a caterpillar becoming a butterfly an example of?
options: Metamorphosis during a life cycle
Photosynthesis in animal cells
Hibernation inside a seed coat
Camouflage turning into migration
explanation: Metamorphosis is a major body-form change across life stages. Butterflies are a classic example.
theoryLines: Life-cycle stages can look very different.
Each stage may have different needs.

stem: Why can camels survive well in desert conditions?
options: They conserve water and tolerate heat well
They need constant rainforest rainfall
They breathe only with fish gills
They hibernate under sea ice
explanation: Desert specialists manage heat and limited water. Camels are classic examples of such adaptations.
theoryLines: Extreme habitats demand extreme adaptations.
Behavior and body traits both matter.

stem: Why can you feel a pulse?
options: Blood surges through arteries with each heartbeat
Bones vibrate from photosynthesis
Hair follicles beat like drums
Skin cells pump oxygen into the air
explanation: Arterial pulses match heartbeats. Feeling pulse is a simple way to monitor heart rate.
theoryLines: Pulse points include wrist and neck.
Heart rate responds to activity and rest.

stem: Why are nutrients from food important for your body?
options: Provide energy and materials for growth and repair
Replace the need for oxygen completely
Turn blood into plant sap
Stop cells from ever needing water
explanation: Proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, and minerals each play roles. Balanced eating supports body function.
theoryLines: Digestion releases nutrients for absorption.
Different foods supply different nutrient mixes.

stem: What is one important job of the liver?
options: It helps process nutrients and clean many harmful substances from the blood.
It pumps air into the lungs with each breath.
It stores urine made by the skin.
It replaces the need for a digestive system.
explanation: The liver is a busy chemical factory. It processes nutrients and helps manage toxins and wastes in the blood.
theoryLines: Organ systems share overlapping jobs.
A healthy lifestyle supports liver function.

stem: Why might one unusual trial not be enough to trust a conclusion?
options: A single result could be a mistake or random chance.
Unusual trials always prove the hypothesis.
Science never uses more than one measurement.
Repeating trials is against lab rules.
explanation: Outliers happen. More trials help you see whether a pattern is real or just noise.
theoryLines: Sample size and repeats matter.
Investigate possible errors when results look odd.

stem: Why is it important to leave nesting wildlife alone?
options: Disturbance can cause parents to abandon eggs or young.
Nests explode when photographed from far away.
Young animals never need protection.
Nests are not part of animal survival strategies.
explanation: Breeding success depends on quiet, safe nesting sites. People can watch respectfully from a distance.
theoryLines: Human behavior affects wildlife outcomes.
Laws often protect nests of certain species.

stem: In a food chain, what do producers provide for the rest of the living things?
options: Food energy made from sunlight
Only shade and cooler air
Nothing useful for animals
Only rocks and minerals
explanation: Producers such as plants capture sunlight and make food. That food energy then moves to animals that eat plants and to animals that eat other animals.
theoryLines: Producers make food using sunlight.
Energy moves from producers to consumers along a food chain.

stem: What is one important job of the skin?
options: Protect the body and help sense touch
Make light for night vision
Pump blood to the lungs
Digest food in the mouth
explanation: Skin is a protective covering. It also helps with touch sensing and helps control body temperature.
theoryLines: Skin is the body's outer protective layer.
Nerve endings in the skin detect touch, heat, and pain.

stem: What does your pulse mainly tell you about?
options: How fast your heart is beating
How long your hair is growing
How much light your eyes store
How thick your skin feels
explanation: A pulse is the throb you feel when blood is pushed by each heartbeat. Counting it shows heart rate.
theoryLines: Pulse rate rises during exercise and strong feelings.
Heartbeats push waves of blood through arteries.

stem: Why is drinking water important for your body?
options: It helps keep your body working and feeling well
It replaces the need to breathe
It turns muscles into stone
It stops you from ever resting
explanation: Water helps your body stay hydrated so cells and organs can do their jobs.
theoryLines: People need water every day.
Thirst is a signal that your body needs fluid.

stem: What is an important job of bones in the body?
options: Support the body and protect soft organs
Digest food in the stomach
Carry smells to the nose
Make rain clouds form
explanation: Bones form the skeleton, which holds you up and helps protect parts such as the brain and heart.
theoryLines: The skeleton gives the body shape.
Bones and muscles work together for movement.

stem: Why is it important to brush your teeth every day?
options: To remove food particles and harmful bacteria that can cause cavities and tooth decay.
To make your teeth grow longer and stronger more quickly.
To help your lungs breathe better throughout the day.
To help the heart pump blood more easily to the rest of the body.
explanation: Brushing your teeth removes food particles and bacteria. If left on the teeth, bacteria produce acids that cause cavities and tooth decay.

stem: Why is sleep important for your body?
options: It helps your body rest and recover
It digests food without any organs
It replaces circulating blood with air
It turns bones into rubber
explanation: During sleep, the body rests and recovers so you can grow, learn, and feel ready for a new day.
theoryLines: Kids need enough sleep each night.
Rest supports a healthy body and mind.

stem: Why are fins important for fish?
options: They help fish swim, steer, and keep balance
They turn water into dry land
They make fish breathe through feathers
They stop fish from ever moving
explanation: Fins are body parts that help fish move through water and stay steady.
theoryLines: Different fins have different jobs in swimming.
Fish bodies are adapted for life in water.

stem: What is pollen's important role for flowering plants?
options: It helps plants reproduce by reaching other flowers
It turns roots into metal wires
It stops photosynthesis forever
It replaces water in every plant
explanation: Pollen carries material needed for seed production when it moves to the right part of a flower.
theoryLines: Pollination is needed for many plants to make seeds.
Wind and animals can move pollen.

stem: Why does exercise help the heart stay healthy?
options: It gives the circulatory system a helpful workout
It stops blood from moving at all
It removes the need for oxygen
It turns the heart into bone
explanation: Regular activity makes the heart stronger so it can pump blood more effectively.
theoryLines: Exercise raises heart rate for a while.
A strong heart supports overall fitness.

stem: Why is protecting habitats important for animals?
options: Animals need habitat resources like food, water, and shelter
Animals can live well with no habitat at all
Habitats are useful only for making noise
Protecting land removes all living things
explanation: When habitats stay healthy, animals can find what they need to survive and reproduce.
theoryLines: Habitat loss threatens many species.
Conservation helps protect ecosystems.

stem: Which sequence shows a butterfly's life cycle?
options: Egg, caterpillar, pupa, adult butterfly
Seed, root, flower, fruit only
Egg, adult bird, nest, feather
Tadpole, fish, shark, whale
explanation: Butterflies go through complete metamorphosis: egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa, and adult.
theoryLines: Metamorphosis means a big change in body form.
Each stage has a different job in the life cycle.

stem: Why is it important to brush your teeth at least twice a day?
options: Brushing removes bacteria and food particles that cause tooth decay and gum disease
Brushing helps the digestive system break down food faster in the stomach
Brushing increases the amount of air that flows into your lungs
Brushing increases blood flow to your brain and improves memory
explanation: Brushing your teeth removes harmful bacteria and food particles, preventing cavities and gum disease and keeping your mouth healthy.

stem: What is one important benefit of getting enough sleep?
options: The body can rest and recover for the next day
Digestion becomes unnecessary
Circulation permanently stops
Bones dissolve overnight
explanation: Sleep helps the body and brain recover so you can learn, grow, and stay healthy.
theoryLines: Kids generally need more sleep than adults.
Rest is part of a healthy lifestyle.

stem: Why should meals include a variety of healthy foods?
options: Different foods supply different nutrients the body needs
Eating only candy gives every nutrient
Food variety removes the need for water
Nutrients are unrelated to growth
explanation: A balanced diet provides proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, and minerals in useful amounts.
theoryLines: No single food has every nutrient you need.
Healthy eating supports energy and growth.

stem: What role do teeth play at the beginning of the digestive process, and why does this step matter for the rest of digestion?
options: They break food into smaller pieces, creating more surface area so digestive juices can work more efficiently throughout the digestive system.
They produce saliva on their own, and that saliva is the only chemical step needed before nutrients pass directly into the bloodstream.
They pump digestive acid upward from the stomach into the mouth to chemically soften food before it is swallowed.
They generate heat that warms and softens food so the small intestine can absorb it without any further breakdown.
explanation: Teeth chew and grind food into small pieces. This mechanical breakdown increases the total surface area of the food, which allows digestive juices — including enzymes in saliva and stomach acid — to reach more of the food and break it down more efficiently. Without this first step, chemical digestion would be much slower and less complete.
theoryLines: Digestion begins in the mouth: teeth provide mechanical breakdown while saliva begins chemical digestion of starches.
Breaking food into smaller pieces increases surface area, making it easier for digestive enzymes in the stomach and small intestine to do their work.

stem: Why must measurements include units?
options: Units tell what the number means so others can compare it
Units hide the true size of objects
Units make tools stop working
Units replace the need for safety
explanation: A number without a unit is unclear. Saying 5 centimeters is different from saying 5 kilograms.
theoryLines: Standard units help people share data.
Always write the unit with the number.

stem: What should a careful observation include?
options: Details about what you actually see, hear, or measure
Only opinions with no evidence
Changed numbers to look perfect
A conclusion written before any test
explanation: Good observations stick to evidence from senses and instruments.
theoryLines: Observations come first; conclusions come later.
Clear notes help other people understand your work.

stem: How do fins help a fish survive?
options: They help the fish swim and keep its balance
They let the fish breathe on dry land only
They turn water into fresh air instantly
They grow feathers for flying
explanation: Fins are swimming adaptations that help fish move through water.
theoryLines: Fish bodies are shaped for aquatic life.
Movement helps fish find food and escape danger.

stem: Which trait belongs to birds but not to fish?
options: Feathers
Gills for underwater breathing
Scales covering the whole body
Living only underwater forever
explanation: Feathers are a key bird trait. Fish typically have scales and use gills in water.
theoryLines: Comparing traits helps identify animal groups.
Birds and fish are adapted to different habitats.

stem: Why is pollen important to flowering plants?
options: It is needed for plants to reproduce and make seeds
It cools the sun each night
It replaces soil for every root
It stops insects from visiting flowers
explanation: When pollen reaches the right flower parts, seeds can form and a new plant generation can begin.
theoryLines: Pollination connects flowers for reproduction.
Bees and other animals often help move pollen.

stem: What is one important job of the skin?
options: It protects the body and helps you feel touch
It digests food in the stomach
It pumps blood like the heart
It makes all of your bones
explanation: Skin covers and protects the body. Nerve endings in skin help you sense touch, heat, and pain.
theoryLines: Skin is the body's outer covering.
Touch sensors in skin send messages to the brain.

stem: Which habits help keep the body healthy?
options: Eating well, moving often, resting, and staying clean
Never drinking water
Skipping sleep every night
Avoiding all fruits and vegetables forever
explanation: Healthy routines support energy, growth, and strong body systems.
theoryLines: Lifestyle choices affect health.
Exercise, sleep, and nutrition work together.

stem: Which organ is an important part of the digestive system?
options: The stomach
The eyelashes
The fingernails
The outer ear only
explanation: The stomach helps break food down so nutrients can be absorbed later.
theoryLines: Digestion begins in the mouth and continues in the stomach and intestines.
Digestive organs work as a team.

stem: What is a healthy habit for your eyes?
options: Take breaks from screens and avoid staring at bright glare
Look directly at the sun for a long time
Rub dirt into your eyes each morning
Never blink during the day
explanation: Protecting eyes from strain and bright glare helps keep vision comfortable and safer.
theoryLines: Eyes are delicate sense organs.
Good lighting and breaks support eye comfort.

stem: What is true about sleep for growing kids?
options: Sleep helps the body grow and recover
Sleep is useless for health
Sleep replaces all food needs
Sleep stops the brain from learning forever
explanation: During sleep, the body repairs itself and supports growth and memory.
theoryLines: Kids usually need plenty of nighttime sleep.
A regular bedtime supports better rest.

stem: Which organs are a major part of the body's waste-filtering system?
options: The kidneys
The eyebrows
The toenails
The earlobes
explanation: Kidneys filter wastes from blood and help make urine.
theoryLines: The excretory system removes wastes.
Healthy kidneys support internal balance.

stem: What is an important job of the small intestine?
options: Absorb digested nutrients into the blood
Pump air into the lungs
Store unused sunlight
Make all of the body's bones
explanation: After food is broken down, the small intestine absorbs nutrients so they can travel through the blood.
theoryLines: Digestion prepares nutrients for absorption.
Blood carries absorbed nutrients to cells.

stem: What is a healthy way to care for yourself when you have a cold?
options: Rest, drink fluids, and keep hands clean
Share drinks with everyone at school
Skip sleep for several nights
Rub dirt into your nose
explanation: Rest and fluids help your body recover. Clean hands help stop germs from spreading.
theoryLines: Hygiene helps protect you and others.
The body needs energy to fight illness.

stem: What can you observe about your pulse after jumping jacks?
options: It usually beats faster than at rest
It permanently disappears
It measures only hair length
It turns into a smell signal
explanation: Activity makes the heart work harder, so pulse rate increases for a while.
theoryLines: Pulse rate is a useful health observation.
After rest, pulse often returns toward normal.

stem: Why is it important to put trash in a trash bin?
options: It keeps our surroundings clean and prevents animals from getting hurt by litter
Trash bins are only decoration and do not actually help the environment
Leaving trash outside is fine because rain washes it all away quickly
The sun will break down all garbage outdoors before it causes any harm
explanation: Throwing trash in a bin keeps the environment clean, prevents animals from eating harmful waste, and stops litter from polluting soil and water.

stem: What do plants need to grow and stay healthy?
options: Water and sunlight
Only packaged nutrients bought from a store
Salt water and deep shade to grow well
Sand and freezing cold weather to survive
explanation: Plants need water and sunlight to carry out photosynthesis, the process they use to make their own food and grow.

stem: Why is it important to save water and not waste it?
options: Fresh water is a limited resource and all living things need it to survive
There is so much water on Earth that it can never run out
Saving water and saving sunlight are exactly the same thing
Water only comes from rivers and cannot be found underground or recycled
explanation: Although Earth has a lot of water, only a small amount is fresh and clean enough for living things to use, so it is important to use it carefully.

stem: Why should empty bottles be recycled when possible?
options: Recycling helps reuse materials and reduce waste
Recycling makes litter grow faster
Recycling removes all oxygen from air
Recycling turns parks into deserts
explanation: Recycling keeps useful materials in use and can reduce trash that harms the environment.
theoryLines: Reduce, reuse, and recycle help the planet.
Sorting recyclables correctly matters.

stem: What causes daytime?
options: Earth rotating so that our part of the planet faces toward the Sun.
The Moon moving in front of the Sun and reflecting light downward.
The Sun traveling around Earth once every 24 hours.
Rain clouds moving away to let sunlight through.
explanation: Earth spins on its own axis once every 24 hours. When the part of Earth where you live turns to face the Sun, sunlight reaches you and it becomes daytime. As Earth continues spinning, that same part faces away from the Sun and it becomes night.
theoryLines: Earth's rotation — its spin on its axis — is what creates the cycle of day and night.
The Sun does not move around Earth; Earth's spin just makes it look that way from the ground.

stem: Why is recycling important?
options: It reduces waste and helps reuse valuable materials
It creates more ocean litter on purpose
It removes all plants from forests
It makes clean air disappear
explanation: Recycling keeps materials in use longer and can lessen pollution and landfill trash.
theoryLines: Recycling works best when materials are sorted correctly.
Reduce and reuse are also helpful habits.
